## Chronological account: GPT-5 (high) formatting failures in GDPval (§3.4, App. A.3)

A note on the source before the narrative: the referenced material is not a single recorded trajectory with a step-by-step tool log. It is an aggregate evaluation write-up. §3.3–3.4 and Appendix A.3 describe a *population* of GPT-5 (high reasoning effort) runs across the GDPval gold subset, the failure modes the graders observed across those runs, and the prompt/scaffolding changes OpenAI then applied. I reconstruct the chronology at that level, citing only what the paper states.

### The task and setup
- **What the agent was asked to do.** GDPval consists of real-world, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks drawn from 44 occupations. Each task is a "request" (frequently bundled with reference files) plus an expected "deliverable" (a finished work product). The graded "gold subset" is 220 tasks (drawn from the full 1,320), authored and reviewed by industry experts averaging 14 years of experience. Deliverables span visual, file-based formats — the prompt later enumerates PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, ZIP, etc.
- **The agent under analysis.** GPT-5 at high reasoning effort, run in a custom harness. For the OpenAI models the harness enabled the **web search tool** and the **code interpreter tool**, with background sampling, and several extra Python libraries were preinstalled in the container.
- **How outputs were judged.** Blind pairwise comparison: occupational experts were shown the request plus reference files and two or more unlabeled deliverables and asked to rank them against the human expert's deliverable. Each prompt was sampled 3 times and each sample graded by 3 experts (9 comparisons per prompt per model across the 220 tasks).

### What the runs produced (the observed behavior)
- **GPT-5 generated the requested deliverable files** using the code interpreter (PDFs, PowerPoint decks, spreadsheets, etc.), and on the substance it did well: §3.3's clustering pipeline (built from expert justifications for why a deliverable was preferred or rejected) found that GPT-5 high had the **fewest instruction-following issues** of the models compared and was among the **fewest accuracy errors** (correct calculations, following instructions). Its strengths showed up especially on pure-text deliverables.
- **The deliverables it produced were frequently malformed at the rendering/formatting layer.** §3.4 states that "many of the observed GPT-5 failure modes were due to obvious formatting errors." Specifically:
  - **Black-square artifacts** appeared in GPT-5's generated PDFs, affecting **over half** of the PDFs it produced.
  - **Egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files** occurred in **86%** of cases.
- **The agent generally did not look at its own output.** Only **15%** of agents used their multimodal capability to inspect the rendered deliverable before submitting. So the artifacts and layout errors were produced and submitted without the model viewing the rendered file as an image.

### The signal/feedback the graders gave
- Because grading is blind pairwise vs. a human deliverable, the "feedback" is the expert preference and written justification. §3.3 reports that whereas Claude, Grok, and Gemini lost mostly on instruction-following, **GPT-5 high "lost mainly from formatting errors."** In other words, GPT-5's competitive losses were concentrated not in being wrong, but in producing deliverables that rendered badly.
- Severity breakdown (App. A.2.6, Fig. 14): GPT-5 failures were most commonly rated "acceptable but subpar"; roughly **29%** were "bad" or "catastrophic" (~3% catastrophic); ~23% were cases where graders thought the model was actually better than the human.

### Where things went wrong
The breakdown was at the final production/verification stage rather than the reasoning stage: GPT-5 correctly followed instructions and did the calculations, then emitted files (PDFs with black squares, PowerPoints with layout errors), and submitted them **without rendering the files to images to check them** — so visible defects (cut-off/overlapping/blank/illegible content, non-portable unicode like U+2011, non-cross-platform fonts, PDF-library artifacts) survived into the graded deliverable and cost it expert preference.

### What was changed in response, and the outcome
OpenAI treated this as an elicitation problem and made two changes (§3.4, with the full prompt in App. A.3):
1. **A general-purpose prompt** (not overfit to any task) instructing the agent to: avoid nonstandard unicode (use U+002D not U+2011), avoid emojis/special characters, keep diagrams legible (≥ half page width), **create PDFs with LibreOffice** (to avoid library artifacts), use cross-platform fonts (Noto Sans/Serif or embed the font), keep deliverable text concise (≤4 sentences, no links), and — centrally — perform **mandatory formatting checks**: convert every visual deliverable to per-page/per-slide PNGs via LibreOffice, **display and visually inspect each PNG**, run programmatic checks for blank/cut-off/overlapping content and page limits, match the deliverable against the request's instructions, and do a final pre-submission integrity check, then emit a `CONFIDENCE[XX]` score.
2. **Scaffolding changes**: enabling GET requests in the container, and best-of-N sampling with **N=4 and a GPT-5 judge**.

Outcome after these changes:
- **Black-square artifacts were fully eliminated.**
- **Egregious PowerPoint formatting errors dropped 86% → 64%.**
- **Use of multimodal self-inspection jumped 15% → 97%.**
- **Human preference win rate rose ~5 percentage points** (Fig. 9b).

The paper frames this as evidence that the formatting failures were "easy" gains — addressable by prompting/scaffolding the agent to be more thorough and to use its multimodal capabilities to inspect its own deliverables.

- [GDPval paper (OpenAI CDN PDF)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/d5eb7428-c4e9-4a33-bd86-86dd4bcf12ce/GDPval.pdf)
